title: Synergistic optimization of strength and ductility in layered ferrite-martensite dual-phase steel
abstract:
The development of ultrafine-grained (UFG) structural materials with high yield strength and superior ductility is crucial for the exploitation of marine energy.
                  This study employed a synergistic regulation strategy involving intercritical quenching and large-strain warm rolling (WR) to prepare a UFG layered ferrite-martensite (F-M) structure steel. The test steel exhibited a high yield strength of 830 ± 10 MPa, while maintaining an elongation of 23.7 %. The excellent performance is attributed to the significant dislocation strengthening effect induced by WR. This effect effectively reduces the hardness difference between microstructures (ΔHV < 1.2 GPa), thereby promoting coordinated deformation. Simultaneously, under the mutual constraint of a layered heterostructure, the dispersed shear bands (SBs) are activated and dynamically propagated, promoting uniform strain distribution and thereby sustaining homogeneous plastic deformation. Additionally, compared with equiaxed grains, the layered heterostructure possesses a higher density of F-M grain boundaries and a more matched geometric necessary dislocations (GNDs) accumulation characteristic length (

                     ), promoting the rapid accumulation of GNDs to achieve significant heterogeneous deformation induced (HDI) strengthening (>500 MPa). The superior strength-ductility balance achieved in F-M steel, attained through the optimization of grain size and microstructural distribution, offers a novel strategy for developing high-performance marine steels.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The low carbon micro-alloyed (LCMA) steels are widely applied in fields such as marine engineering platforms due to their reasonable strength-ductility performance and favorable economic benefits  [1–4] . As marine energy exploitation advances into deeper oceanic regions, the structural materials face higher demands for enhanced strength and ductility. While conventional strengthening methods, such as martensitic transformation  [5] , grain refinement  [6,7] , and increased carbon content  [8] , can significantly improve the strength of LCMA steels, they often result in a substantial decline in ductility and strain hardening capacity. To address this dilemma, researchers have been exploring novel microstructural regulation strategies to optimize the strength-ductility balance of LCMA steels, including high-temperature tempering  [9]  and intercritical annealing  [10]  of martensitic and fine-grained structures. However, these microstructures, characterized by high-density dislocations and grain boundaries, are accompanied by softening mechanisms such as martensite dissolution, dislocation recovery, and recrystallization during isothermal treatment, which decrease the material's strength  [11–13] .

Recently, heterostructure materials comprising soft and hard zone structural units have garnered attention for their superior synergy of strength and ductility. During plastic deformation, the strain mismatch between the soft and hard phases leads to the accumulation of GNDs near the HS interfaces, resulting in pronounced HDI hardening  [14] . It is considered one of the most effective strengthening mechanisms for avoiding a substantial sacrifice of material ductility  [15,16] . This mechanism not only effectively delays the onset of plastic instability and necking but also imparts HS materials with superior strain-hardening capability compared to homogeneous materials. For instance, a CoCrNi medium-entropy alloy with a HS of multi-level grains, formed through cold rolling and annealing, achieved a yield strength of 1 GPa and a uniform elongation of 22 %  [17] . Moreover, Zhang et al. introduced multiscale HS that include bimodal grain size distributions, submicron spherical C14 phases, and nanoscale atomic clusters in high-entropy alloys, which have achieved unusual secondary hardening that enhanced the uniform elongation and work hardening rate to 13.7 % and 1.5 GPa, respectively  [18] . Meanwhile, for the 9Cr-1Mo steel with a gradient microstructure prepared via surface mechanical grinding treatment, the nanocrystalline grains in the surface layer maintained substantial plastic strain through reorientation, thereby delaying fracture occurrence  [19] . Compared with other complex preparation processes, the F-M structure prepared by intercritical quenching in LCMA steel is considered to be an ideal HS material due to its significant strength difference  [20,21] .

Studies have revealed that factors such as the strength difference, distribution characteristics, and grain size of the F-M phases can influence the mechanical properties of the material by regulating local strain partitioning behavior  [22–24] . When martensite is distributed continuously in a chain-like pattern along ferrite grain boundaries, the material often exhibits excellent ductility  [25,26] . In contrast, in DP 980 steel, which is dominated by blocky microstructures, the pronounced strength mismatch between the F-M leads to interfacial strain concentration, which induces the nucleation of microcracks  [27,28] . Scott et al. demonstrated through mechanical modeling that reducing martensite strength more significant improvements in ductility  [29] . Park et al. utilized tempering treatment to reduce martensite hardness from 3.56 GPa to 2.95 GPa, and through digital image correlation (DIC) technology, confirmed that enhancing the plastic deformation capacity of martensite effectively alleviates strain localization  [30] . Meanwhile, CHANDIRAN et al. found that the homogeneous dispersion of nano-precipitates in ferrite can effectively increase the strength of dual-phase (DP) steel, while F-M grain refinement is a critical factor in improving uniform elongation  [31] . Therefore, improving strength-ductility through​ structural design in DP steels has become a mainstream approach. In particular,​ layered heterostructures composed of ferrite and martensite phases show significant potential. For instance, Gao et al. successfully prepared layered F-M heterostructures​ through warm rolling and annealing treatments, confirming the pronounced effect of HDI strengthening  [32] . However, when grain size is further refined to the submicron scale in pursuit of higher strength, effectively maintaining material ductility remains a major challenge  [7,33] . More importantly, systematic in-depth research on the deformation coordination mechanisms of UFG layered heterostructures, particularly regarding​ strain distribution, the evolution of GNDs, and their correlation with ultimate damage behavior, is still lacking.

Based on the above analysis, this study proposes an innovative microstructure control strategy that combines intercritical quenching with warm rolling. This approach prepares UFG layered F-M heterostructure steel that exhibits both high strength and excellent ductility. This study will systematically elucidate the coordinated deformation mechanism of layered heterostructures, focusing on the critical roles of HDI strengthening, GNDs accumulation, and dynamic rearrangement of SBs in strain redistribution. Furthermore, by contrasting with traditional equiaxed grain structures, it reveals the intrinsic interplay among microstructural morphology, dislocation motion, strain localization, and damage behavior. This work not only provides valuable insights into the deformation and strengthening mechanisms of layered heterostructure materials but also offers novel strategies for developing next-generation high-performance marine steel.

sections.heading: Materials preparation
Mechanical properties test
paragraphs: Tensile samples (with a length of 110.0 mm, a central diameter of φ 5.0 mm, and a gauge length of 25.0 mm) were prepared parallel to the rolling direction (RD) of the plate. Room temperature tensile tests were repeated three times on the WEMC003A-3a testing machine at a constant strain rate of 1 × 10 −3 /s, and the experimental results were averaged with error calculations.The microhardness of the samples was measured using a G200X nanoindentation instrument. After mechanical polishing, the samples were etched with a 4 % nitric acid-alcohol solution, and 100 measurements were taken under a 5 mN load. During data processing, invalid data points caused by factors such as sample height were removed. The cyclic loading–unloading-reloading (LUR) tensile tests were performed on samples (length 132 mm, central diameter φ 6.0 mm, gauge length 40.0 mm) using an Instron 5982 testing machine. The samples were stretched to predetermined strains at a strain rate of 1 × 10 −3 /s, unloaded to 100 N, and then reloaded at the same strain rate. Prior to the in-situ SEM-DIC experiments, the transverse plane of the dog-bone-shaped samples was ground, polished, and etched with a 4 % nitric acid-alcohol solution. In-situ tensile testing was conducted using a micro-loading stage integrated within an SEM system (FIB/SEM, Zeiss Auriga) at a constant displacement rate of 1 µm/s. SEM images of the same location were captured at different strain levels. The inherent fine-scale contrast in the etched microstructure of F-M steel served as a natural speckle pattern for DIC calculations, which is a method previously employed in DIC analysis  [21,34] . The equivalent plastic strain distribution in WR steel was then quantitatively analyzed using ARAMIS software (GOM GmbH) with a subset size of 14 × 14 pixel 2 . In addition, for the rod-shaped sample (length 132 mm, center diameter φ 6.0 mm, gauge length 40.0 mm), it was necessary to spray a random speckle pattern on the surface before the DIC (CSI) test to identify the deformation information. During the experiment, the speckle displacement image of the sample surface was taken with a high-speed camera at an interval of 450 ms. The image were processed into strain distribution data using VIC2D software, and the size of the image-related pixel subset is 20 × 20 pixel 2 .

sections.heading: Microstructural characterization
paragraphs: The samples were ground, polished, and then etched with a 4 vol% nitric acid in ethanol solution. Subsequent microstructural characterization was performed using​ SEM (Sirion 200), and elemental distribution was analyzed via​ an electron probe micro-analyzer (EPMA, EPMA-8050G). Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, Oxford/Symmetry, UK) was employed for microstructure characterization under the following operating conditions: acceleration voltage of 20 kV, beam current of 13nA, working distance of 10 mm, tilt angle of 70°, and step size of 0.08 μm. The samples were electropolished in a mixed solution of 5 vol% perchloric acid and 95 vol% ethanol to relieve stress, with an applied voltage of 25 V for approximately 30 S. The TEM samples were mechanically ground to 70 μm, followed by twin-jet electropolishing using an electrolyte solution (10 % perchloric acid + 90 % acetic acid). The thinned samples were then examined using a transmission electron microscope (TEM, CF-HR/JEM-F200, Japan) equipped with an Energy-Dispersive Spectrometer (EDS, Oxford/Aztec Ultim Live 100X, UK) for microstructure characterization and elemental distribution analysis. High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) was further employed to investigate the microstructural features. The HRTEM results were processed using Digital Micrograph software, and the data were indexed and analyzed using the corresponding cif file as referenced in Ref  [35] . TEM samples were also used for transmission Kikuchi diffraction (TKD) experiments in a scanning electron microscope (ThermoFisher Helios 5 CX DualBeam) equipped with an electron backscatter diffraction detector (Symmetry S3 EBSD). During TKD analysis, the working voltage was set at 30 KV, the current at 11nA, and a step size of 0.012 μm was selected. AZtecCrystal software was employed for post-processing and analysis of the EBSD and TKD data. The misorientation angles with 5 − 15 ◦  and ≥ 15 ◦  are defined as low angle grain boundaries (LAGBs) and high angle grain boundaries (HAGBs), respectively. Elemental diffusion during isothermal processes was simulated using Thermo-Calc software and its DICTRA module with TCFE10 thermodynamic database and MOBFE6 kinetic database.

sections.heading: Microstructure characterization
paragraphs:
Fig. 2a 
                          shows the thickness variations of the steel tested before and after warm rolling, as well as the sampling locations for microstructural characterization. The inverse pole figures (IPFs) in  Figs. 2b and e  depict the grain morphology and crystal orientation; the grains exhibit preferred orientations of <001> and <111> after warm rolling. The band contrast (BC) map of the QLT sample shows a mixed distribution of fine grains (FG) and coarse grains (CG). The microstructure consists of granular martensite (GM), lath ferrite (LF), and polygonal ferrite (PF), with fine martensite grains predominantly distributed along the ferrite grain boundaries ( Fig. 2c ). The statistics map of effective grain size shows the bimodal distribution of CG (15.4 ± 3.7 μm) and FG (4.9 ± 1.3 μm) ( Fig. 2h ). After warm rolling treatment, the microstructure is transformed into a uniform layered structure, and the effective grain size is refined to 1.5 ± 0.6 μm ( Figs. 2e and i ). At the same time, numerous sub-grain boundaries are formed in the grains. Compared with the QLT sample, the WR sample exhibits a higher proportion of LAGBs, increasing from 18.4 % to 35.3 % ( Figs. 2c and f ).

Figs. 2d and g  are grain reference orientation deviation (GROD) maps used to reflect the internal strain distribution within grains. The GROD distribution maps show that the proportion of grains with high strain concentration (red and green regions) in the WR sample is higher than that in the QLT sample. The average GROD values for the two samples are 9.61° and 3.28°, respectively. This difference is mainly due to the rapid multiplication and accumulation of dislocations during warm rolling  [19] .

The EPMA analysis reveals the distribution of C and Mn elements in both test steels ( Fig. 3 ). Results show that in the QLT sample, martensite regions exhibit higher concentrations of C and Mn compared to ferrite regions ( Fig. 3. 
                         a − c). In contrast, the WR sample exhibits more uniform distributions of C and Mn ( Fig. 3. d − f). This phenomenon is attributed to the enhanced elemental diffusion from​ the higher density of defects (such as dislocations and sub-grain boundaries) induced during the rolling process  [7] . The reduction in elemental concentration gradient typically contributes to decreased hardness differences between martensite and ferrite phases, thereby promoting the coordinated deformation of the two phases  [36] .

TEM was used to characterize the microstructure evolution and dislocation distribution before and after warm rolling ( Fig. 4 
                         ). In the QLT sample, the martensite with high dislocation density is mainly distributed along the ferrite grain boundaries, and there are fine lath structures inside the grains ( Fig. 4a ). Numerous carbides precipitated at the martensite regions and grain boundaries after the tempering treatment ( Fig. 4b ). The corresponding selected area electron diffraction (SAED) patterns from the martensite region (indicated by the red circle in  Fig. 4b ) are shown in  Fig. 4c .​ These carbides facilitate the refinement of grains along the rolling direction by pinning grain boundaries during the subsequent warm rolling process. After warm rolling treatment, microstructure exhibit a layered structure with significant grain refinement ( Fig. 4d ). The widths of the ferrite and martensite layers were statistically measured as 288.7 ± 38.8 nm and 171.9 ± 25.2 nm, respectively ( Fig. 4e ). Furthermore, the ferrite undergoes severe plastic deformation, resulting in the formation of a high density of dislocations network ( Fig. 4f ).

The TKD was used to analyze the orientation and strain distribution within ferrite layers.  Fig. 4g  shows the presence of diverse orientations within a single ferrite layer, and grains (G 1  and G 2 ) were selected for texture analysis. Based on Euler angle calculations, these were identified as {112}<110>and {111}<112> texture components, both of which are typical texture formations in body-centered cubic (BCC) steels during warm rolling and annealing. This is consistent with the strong γ-fiber texture observed in the WR sample (Fig. S1).​ Among these, {111} < 112 > is considered to make significant contributions to the improvement of material ductility  [37] . The distribution map of kernel average misorientation (KAM) reveals that cross-distributed deformation bands form within coarser ferrite layers ( Fig. 4h ). The cumulative misorientation (point to origin) in high-strain regions (along the white solid line in  Fig. 4h ) exhibits a stepwise increase, confirming the formation of sub-grain boundaries within the ferrite, a key mechanism for​ strain hardening ( Fig. 4i ).

sections.heading: Mechanical properties
paragraphs:
Fig. 5a 
                          shows the stress–strain curve of the QLT sample, which exhibits an arched shape, exhibiting a continuous yield behavior (Eng, Engineering stress–strain; True, True stress–strain). The WR sample displays obvious Lüders bands during deformation, a characteristic of​ discontinuous yield. Due to the premature yield of coarse-grained ferrite (CG-F), the QLT sample displays lower yield strength (502 ± 6 MPa) and higher total elongation (30.9 ± 0.8 %). The yield strength of the WR sample increases to 830 ± 10 MPa, marking a substantial improvement of approximately 65 % compared to the QLT sample, while maintaining an elongation of 23.7 ± 0.5 % ( Table 2 
                         , YS, yield strength; UTS, ultimate tensile strength; TEL, total elongation; UE, uniform elongation).  Fig. 5b  presents a comparative analysis of the strength-ductility properties between various dual-phase steels and marine steels with similar compositions. The results demonstrate that the WR sample with the UFG layered structure design achieves an outstanding strength-ductility synergy, showing superior elongation compared to steels of equivalent strength grade (with a yield strength of about 800 MPa)  [3–5,10,26,27,37–46] .

Fig. 5c  shows the strain hardening rate (SHR) curve of the test steel, and the plastic deformation process is divided into two stages based on its slope variations. The QLT sample exhibits a peak in SHR during Stage I, followed by a sharp decline. In the WR sample, the first stage of strain hardening primarily corresponds to the formation of Lüders bands, where the SHR remains relatively low and fluctuates consistently, finally decreasing rapidly. Upon entering Stage II, the SHR slowly decreases until the material undergoes necking and fracture. The extent of strain during Stage II is generally linked to the ductility of the material  [18] . Specifically, the QLT sample displays a broader range of steady-state strain (ε = 0.035–0.19), whereas the WR sample exhibits a narrower range of steady-state deformation (ε = 0.065–0.13).

The evolution of the strain field during tensile process was characterized and analyzed using DIC technology. The results show that the WR sample exhibits localized strain concentration at the initial stage of deformation, which progressively evolves into stable high-strain deformation bands under continued tensile loading, ultimately leading to sample fracture (indicated by white dashed arrows in  Fig. 5 d1). Furthermore, the Lüders band stripe inclined at a 45° angle to the loading direction during the initial deformation stage (approximately 4 % strain), indicating a distinct deformation orientation​ (yellow arrows in  Fig. 5 d2). Although the QLT sample also exhibits local strain concentration during early deformation, the strain progressively diffuses to the surrounding matrix as deformation proceeds (marked by white circles and dashed lines in  Fig. 5 d3), showing a strain-buffering phenomenon. This dynamic strain redistribution behavior effectively delays the initiation and propagation of microcracks caused by stress concentration, thereby improving the ductility of the material  [47] .

sections.heading: Microhardness and HDI stress measurements
paragraphs:
The superior strength-ductility synergy in heterostructure materials is usually attributed to the significant HDI strengthening effect  [48] . However, the HDI strengthening effect is not simply proportional to the strength difference in heterostructures, but is influenced by multiple factors such as dislocation density, grain size distribution, and deformation mechanisms  [16,49] . Therefore, significant HDI strengthening can still be achieved in some HS materials even when their strength difference is relatively small  [50] . To quantitatively evaluate the hardness difference in the present materials,​ nanoindentation tests were carried out to assess the microhardness of the samples. Due to the fine grain size, which made it impossible to accurately measure the hardness of individual phases, 100 hardness tests were conducted to analyze microhardness variations. Invalid data points caused by surface imperfections​ were removed, and the results were ​plotted in ascending order. The results demonstrate that the WR sample exhibits a more uniform hardness distribution, with the maximum hardness differential (ΔHv) decreasing from 1.7 GPa to 1.2 GPa ( Fig. 6a 
                         ). This validates that warm rolling enhances the strength of ferrite, thereby reducing the hardness difference between the two phases and promoting​ excellent deformation coordination during tensile deformation  [51] .

The HDI stress value was evaluated through LUR tensile tests.  Figs. 6b and 6c  display the LUR true stress–strain curves and the hysteresis loops, respectively. The WR sample exhibits a wider hysteresis loop, indicating that the layered F-M induces a stronger Bauschinger effect, thereby generating higher HDI stress.                           represent the HDI stress, reloading yield stress and unloading yield stress, respectively.  Fig. 6d  shows the HDI stress calculation results of test steels. Compared with the QLT sample, the WR sample exhibits a higher HDI stress, exceeding 50 % of the flow stress at the initial deformation stage. This is primarily attributed to the high density of GNDs generated by the warm rolling process, as well as the concurrent refinement of​ ferrite grains. As shown in Fig. S2, the GNDs density in the WR sample is as high as 8.2 × 10 15  m −2 , more than twice that of the QLT sample. Within the strain range of 3 % – 9 %, the HDI stress increases rapidly with the deformation amount. When the strain exceeds 9 %, the HDI stress stabilizes​ due to the reduced multiplication rate of GNDs from​ the increased hardening​ of ferrite ( Fig. 6d ).

sections.heading: Microstructural evolution during deformation
paragraphs:
Fig. 7 
                          shows the microstructural morphology of the sample at a strain of 3 %. In the QLT sample, the high strength of the martensite causes plastic deformation to concentrated primarily in the CG-F grains, leading to the formation of high-density dislocation tangles ( Fig. 7a ). The deformation incompatibility between the two phases generates a significant strain gradient at the interface, which drives the accumulation of a large number of GNDs on the ferrite side and results in local strain concentration. In the KAM distribution map, the central regions of CG-F grains exhibit the lowest KAM values, with higher strain concentrations observed at the interfaces between CG-F and fine-grained martensite (FG-M), indicating that CG-F grains display significant deformation inhomogeneity ( Figs. 7b and c ).

Figs. 7d and e  show the formation of dense dislocation networks within the ferrite layers of the WR sample after deformation, indicating that dislocation multiplication and interaction are more active. As the width of the ferrite layers increases, the dislocation mobility and multiplication efficiency increase. Comparative analysis shows that the dislocation density in G 2  grains is notably lower than that in the relatively coarser G 1  and G 3  grains ( Fig. 7e ). Fine sub-structures were formed in the ferrite grains after deformation. These sub-structures appear as deformation bands with high strain concentration in the KAM map ( Figs. 7f and g ). To analyze​ the deformation inhomogeneity of the F-M structure. After conducting High-Resolution Transmission Electron Micrograph (HRTEM) characterization of the F-M interfaces, Inverse Fast Fourier Transform (IFFT) and Geometric Phase Analysis (GPA) were employed (the IFFT image is shown in the top-right corner of  Fig. 7h ). The results indicate that the strain level in the ferrite is significantly higher than that in the martensite ( Fig. 7i ).

When the strain increases to about 12 %, the ferrite in the QLT sample underwent severe plastic deformation along the load direction, resulting in obvious dislocation tangles at the F-M interface ( Fig. 8a 
                         ). In addition, deformation microbands (DBs) formed in multiple directions within the CG-F, which not only promoted dislocation multiplication but also generated a dense network structure through interactions between dislocations from different bands ( Figs. 8b and c ). This network effectively hinders dislocation motion, thereby enhancing strain hardening capacity  [18] . In contrast, the WR sample underwent severe plastic deformation that caused layer fragmentation. Within the grains, substantial dislocation accumulation and mutual entanglement formed dislocation cells, reducing the mean free path of mobile dislocations ( Figs. 8d and e ).

In addition, Mn and Cr rich M 23 C 6  carbides also have an adverse effect on deformation ( Fig. 8f ). HRTEM characterization​ of the interface between the carbide and the matrix was performed ( Fig. 8g ). The IFTT pattern on the carbide side shows that the carbide contains the Cr 23 C 6  phase, and the (1

                          0) and (220) crystal plane spacing are 0.615 nm and 0.377 nm, respectively ( Fig. 8h ). Due to the higher elastic modulus and deformation resistance of carbides  [52] , a significant strain mismatch with the matrix is developed during deformation. This strain incompatibility was one of the key contributing factors to layer interface cracking ( Fig. 8i ).

sections.heading: Strain partitioning during plastic deformation in WR sample
paragraphs:
The evolution of dislocations during the deformation process of the test steel was related to the uneven distribution of strain between the soft and hard phases  [47] . The strain distribution was dynamically characterized using in-situ SEM and DIC techniques, revealing the strain evolution behavior of the layered F-M structure, as shown in  Fig. 9 
                         . In the undeformed state, the layers were arranged in parallel, with the ferrite geometrically constrained by the adjacent martensite layers in multiple directions ( Fig. 9a ). At 3 % strain, most of the ferrite layers underwent plastic deformation, while the martensite remained elastic, resulting in higher strain borne by the ferrite (as indicated by the yellow arrows in  Fig. 9b ).

When the strain increases to 6 %, the martensite begins to undergo plastic deformation. At this stage, multiple SBs formed in the microstructure, oriented at 40° − 50° relative to the loading direction (as indicated by red arrows in  Fig. 9c ). With a further increase in strain to 9 % −12 %, the continuous propagation of SBs facilitated the participation of more martensite grains in plastic deformation ( Fig. 9 d - e). The strain accommodation mechanism was dominated by the newly formed SBs, particularly within the local ferrite layers (as shown in the black coils distributed along the SBs in  Fig. 9e ). When the deformation reached 15 %, the strain distribution became more homogeneous, with SBs became nearly parallel to the loading direction ( Fig. 9f ). This evolutionary process reveals that dynamic strain redistribution is achieved through shear band rearrangement in the layered F-M structure during deformation.

Fig. 9 g 1  shows a magnified image of the undeformed F-M layers. The local strain distribution along the direction indicated by the red arrow in  Fig. 9 g 1  demonstrates periodic characteristics at 3 %, 9 %, and 15 % strain levels ( Fig. 9 g 2 ). The peak and trough of strain correspond to ferrite and martensite layers, respectively. This regular distribution indicates that the ferrite always bears higher plastic strain, resulting in a significant strain gradient at the F-M interface, which promotes the accumulation of GNDs.

Meanwhile, inhomogeneous plastic deformation is also observed within the ferrite layers. This inhomogeneity is primarily influenced by the dispersed distribution of SBs. As shown in  Fig. 9 h 1  and h 2 , a single ferrite layer is divided by multiple SBs (black dotted lines). The strain distribution along the red arrow direction indicates that the region through which SBs pass shows higher plastic strain ( Fig. 9 h 2  and h 3 ). This micro-scale strain concentration phenomenon not only indicates the strain inhomogeneity inside the ferrite but also reveals the important role of SBs as a strain carrier in regulating the plastic deformation of ferrite layers.

sections.heading: Fracture behavior of WR sample
paragraphs:
After the tensile fracture of the QLT sample, the fracture surface was dominated by uniformly distributed dimples, characteristic of a ductile fracture (Fig. S3). In contrast, the WR sample displayed a delamination morphology with step-like fracture features ( Fig. 10a 
                         ). Near the delamination cracks, alternating regions of ductile and brittle fracture were observed ( Fig. 10 b 1 ), while non-delaminated areas showed typical ductile fracture with numerous dimples ( Fig. 10 b 2 ).  Fig. 10c  reveals that the fracture path of the WR sample during in situ tensile testing formed an angle of approximately 45° with the tensile axis. Multiple coarse cracks (yellow arrows) can be seen on the surface of the sample. At the 3 % strain stage, obvious strain concentration appears around the intergranular carbides, and deformation bands with high KAM values form due to dislocation slip in the grains ( Fig. 10 c 1  and c 2 ).

Fig. 10 c 3  shows that when the strain increases to 9 %, the grain boundary near carbides cracks (yellow dotted line), forming delamination cracks that propagate along the tensile direction, accompanied by secondary crack initiation perpendicular to the layer's direction (green arrow). With a further increase in strain to 15 %, the secondary cracks propagated rapidly, eventually penetrating entire layers and interconnecting adjacent delamination cracks ( Fig. 10 c 4 ). Ultimately, these converging cracks coalesced into macroscopic cracks propagating along the tensile direction, leading to the final sample fracture ( Fig. 10 c 5 ).  Fig. 10d  schematically illustrates the nucleation and propagation processes of both delamination and secondary cracks during deformation.

sections.heading: The formation mechanism of layered F-M structure
paragraphs: To elucidate the evolution process of the layered F-M structure, Q(quenching) – state, QL (quenching and intercritical-quenching)-state, and QT (quenching and tempering)-state samples were prepared, with corresponding SEM maps shown in Fig. S4. Different from the lath structures observed in Q-state and QT-state, the QL samples developed a microstructure dominated by ferrite and martensite. The formation of the F-M structure is attributed to the nucleation and growth of reverse transformed austenite during the intercritical isothermal process, which is influenced by the diffusion and redistribution of C, Mn, and other alloying elements  [39,53] .

The DICTRA kinetic software was employed to simulate the growth behavior of austenite and the diffusion patterns of elements during the isothermal process at 780 °C. Based on TEM characterization results, the model size was set to half the width of a ferrite-martensite unit (2 μm), as illustrated in  Fig. 11a 
                         . In this model, a 1 nm-thick austenite layer was present at the left boundary of the BCC structure as the initial phase, with a movable interface between the two phases. The chemical composition of the initial austenite phase and the BCC matrix were set to 0.1 % and the test steel composition (Fe-0.14C-0.98Mn-1.02Cr, wt.%), respectively.

Fig. 11 b − d show the concentration variations of C, Mn and Cr elements in the two phases during the isothermal process, respectively. The C element in the BCC phase diffuses into the austenite and homogenizes rapidly at 10 −3  s. With the extension of isothermal time to 10 3  s, the C content in austenite gradually stabilized at about 0.19 % ( Fig. 11b ). The diffusion rates of Mn and Cr elements are relatively slow. When the isothermal time reaches 10 s, the concentration of the two phases near the interface begins to fluctuate significantly. As the isothermal time is further extended to 10 3  s, the Mn and Cr distributions in the BCC phase become increasingly uniform. Finally, at the end of isothermal treatment (10 5  s), the concentrations of Mn and Cr in the austenite region near the F-M interface reached 1.42 % and 1.91 %, respectively, significantly higher than those in other regions ( Figs. 11c and d ). The Mn and Cr enriched reversed austenite will undergo martensitic transformation during the subsequent cooling process, and finally the microstructure dominated by martensite and ferrite is formed in the test steel.

Fig. 12 
                          presents the evolution of the layered F-M structure. Taking the Q-state prior austenite grain as an example, it possesses​ multi-scale substructural characteristics with a high density of dislocations (I). Due to the higher concentration of elements (C, Mn, etc.) at substructure boundaries, carbide precipitation preferentially occurs during heating (Stage II). With the extension of isothermal time, carbides gradually dissolve, leading to a significant increase in the concentration of alloying elements in local areas such as substructure boundary and prior austenite grain boundary (GBs). Consequently, these regions become preferential nucleation sites for fibrous reversed austenite (Stage III).

Subsequent austenite continues to coarsen through interface migration and finally reaches a thermodynamic equilibrium state (Stage IV). During the cooling stage, the austenite phase enriched with Mn, Cr, and C transforms into martensite (Stage V). In the warm rolling deformation stage, the microstructure is significantly refined along the rolling direction to form a layered F-M structure. The subsequent annealing process promotes selective carbide precipitation, enabling​ further control of microstructure and properties as well as redistribution of alloying elements (Stage VI).

sections.heading: Deformation and damage mechanism of layered F-M structure
HDI strengthening and strain hardening behavior
paragraphs:
The exceptional strength and ductility of WR samples are primarily attributed to the significant HDI strengthening effect induced by the layered heterostructure and the dynamic rearrangement mechanism of shear bands. Analysis of the microstructure evolution and strain distribution indicates that the differences in deformation behavior between the two groups of test steels stem from​ the following three aspects: (I) dislocation multiplication and slip modes; (II) the distribution characteristics of the F-M phases; and (III) the grain size effect.  Fig. 13 
                             presents​ a schematic diagram illustrating the deformation mechanisms of the tested steel. Firstly, the multiplication and slip behavior of dislocations play a key role in coordinating the strain gradient  [50,54] . The CG-F in​ the QLT sample accommodates​ only a small number of dislocations and lacks effective dislocation pinning points (such as precipitate phases and sub-grain boundaries), resulting in lower HDI stress and yield strength of the sample​ ( Figs. 5a and 6d ).

In contrast, the ferrite grains in WR samples undergo pre-deformation, leading to the formation of high-density dislocations and sub-grain boundaries within the grains (as shown in  Figs. 4d, f , and  Fig. 13 c 1 ), significantly increasing dislocation slip resistance. This results in high yield strength and HDI strengthening effects ( Fig. 5a  and  Fig. 6d ). However, as deformation progresses, the extensive distribution of dislocation walls and dislocation cells severely impedes further dislocation slip ( Figs. 8d and e ). Therefore, relying solely on the dislocation slip mechanism makes it difficult to sustain continuous uniform plastic deformation at high strengths.

In-situ DIC results reveal that when dislocation slip is impeded near​ the F-M phase boundaries, causing​ localized strain concentration, the layered heterostructure can coordinate strain redistribution by activating a network of uniformly distributed​ SBs ( Fig. 13 c 2 ). As deformation increases to 9 %, the SBs network continuously propagates and interconnects, effectively transferring highly concentrated plastic strain from the yielded ferrite to the high-strength martensite layers, promoting uniform strain distribution. This coordinated deformation behavior, driven by​ the dynamic evolution of shear bands, facilitates effective macroscale strain redistribution. Consequently, it delays localized necking phenomena, thereby achieving high strength while maintaining excellent uniform elongation.

Secondly, warm rolling promotes​ compositional homogenization and ferrite refinement, which facilitates​ coordinated deformation between the two phases by reducing microstructural strength variations (ΔHv < 1.2 GPa,  Fig. 5a ). Moreover, grain boundaries act as sources for dislocations  [55] , in comparison to the equiaxed grain structure of the QLT sample, the layered structure design makes the ferrite surrounded by martensite, forming a higher density of F-M grain boundaries. This microstructure exhibits a dual strengthening mechanism during deformation: (1) the strong constraint of martensite inhibits the premature yield of ferrite grains; (2) high-density F-M grain boundaries provide abundant multiplication sites for GNDs, thereby promoting the generation of high HDI stresses ( Fig. 6d ).

sections.heading: Nucleation mechanism of cracks
paragraphs: The distribution characteristics of microstructures and differences in strength not only influence the deformation behavior of samples but also determine the ultimate fracture mode. As shown in  Section 3.6 , WR samples exhibit mixed damage characteristics dominated by ferrite layer cracking and grain boundary delamination. This contrasts with the typical F-M interface debonding-dominated mode observed in QLT samples (Fig. S5). This fundamental difference stems from distinct strain localization mechanisms. In QLT samples, the significant strength difference between phases results in plastic deformation concentration within ferrite grains during the early stages. This generates substantial strain gradients at F-M interfaces, leading to the accumulation of GNDs. Such strain localization at interfaces is the primary cause of interface debonding  [27,56] .

In WR samples, the warm rolling process reduces the hardness difference between phases, promoting coordinated deformation between the phases. Furthermore, the layered structure subjects the ferrite layers to strong geometric constraints from adjacent martensite during deformation. This constraint forces plastic strain to be released locally through the formation of SBs ( Fig. 9 ). Consequently, the primary strain localization mechanism in WR samples shifts from interfacial GND accumulation to SB propagation within ferrite layers. Ultimately, the synergistic effects of SBs induced localized high-strain zones and intergranular carbides, leading to crack nucleation and propagation preferentially via ferrite cracking and grain boundary delamination, forming a unique mixed damage pattern ( Fig. 10 c 3  and c 4 ). This demonstrates that designing layered heterostructures can lead to a shift in damage patterns toward more energy absorbing mechanisms, thereby enhancing the damage tolerance of materials.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs:
In this study, a UFG layered F-M steel with an excellent strength-ductility synergy​ was prepared, and its microstructure evolution, deformation mechanism, and fracture behavior were systematically analyzed. The main conclusions are as follows: 
                         
                            (1) 
                            An ultrafine-grained layered F-M steel (d F : 288.7 ± 38.8 nm, d M : 171.9 ± 25.2 nm) was successfully prepared by large deformation warm rolling of the intercritical quenching sample. The test steel exhibits a high yield strength of 830 ± 10 MPa, marking a 65 % increase compared to the QLT sample, and maintains an elongation of 23.7 %, which effectively alleviates the trade-off dilemma between strength and ductility in LCMA steel. 
                         
                         
                            (2) 
                            WR sample superior strength and ductility properties are attributed to the high density of F-M interfaces in the layered structure and its more compatible characteristic length for GND accumulation ( 
                                  
                                     l 
                                     
                                        GND 
                                     
                                  
                               ). These features promote​ GNDs multiplication​ and accumulation, thereby inducing​ a significant HDI strengthening effect. Furthermore, the warm rolling process reduces the hardness difference between the microstructure (ΔHv < 1.2 GPa), facilitating coordinated deformation and triggering the formation of diffusely distributed shear bands to sustain uniform plastic deformation of the sample. 
                         
                         
                            (3) 
                            The damage behavior of the F-M steel is governed by its strain localization mechanism. In the QLT sample, strain localization primarily occurs​ through GNDs accumulation at the F-M interfaces, leading to interfacial decohesion as the dominant damage mode. In contrast, in the WR sample, the layered martensite exerts​ a strong constraint on the ferrite. This not only promotes strain localization and dislocation accumulation within the ferrite but also enables dynamic strain redistribution through SBs rearrangements. Under high stress, this results in a mixed damage mode characterized by​ ferrite layer cracking and grain boundary delamination.
